title: Your work, written
hookLine: what is your work, really, beyond the job title?

cards: So, what do you do? It's the first question at a party, and the easy answer is a job title. Accountant.

Retired. The title is true, but it's thin. It doesn't say that the accountant is the one who stays calm when a family's finances fall apart, or that the student is quietly holding a household together.
For weeks this path has looked at work through scripture, craft, festivals and harvest. One question is left: what is your work, really? Today: your work.

teach.b: First, an essayist on calling. Ralph Waldo Emerson, in his essay Spiritual Laws, puts it in two short sentences: "Each man has his own vocation. The talent is the call."
A vocation, in his sense, isn't a title someone hands you. It's what you're fitted for, the one direction, he says, in which all space opens. A title can match it, or only sit somewhere near it.
Second, a job description in one line. The prophet Micah sums up what God asks in a single sentence.

teach.h: DO JUSTLY, LOVE MERCY, WALK HUMBLY.
teach.b: In the King James words: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Three verbs, no job title, and it could sit on top of all sorts of jobs. Third, the gap.

teach.h: THE BADGE AND THE REAL WORK.
teach.b: Between the title and the real work, there's usually a gap. A teacher's title is teacher; her work might be making sure no child feels stupid.
A bus driver's title is driver; his work might be getting tired people home safely, and being a kind face at the end of a long day. The title is what's on the badge.
The real work is what you'd want someone to say you did. Fourth, writing it down.
One line is enough: short enough to remember, plain enough to check against a Tuesday. It isn't a mission statement for a boss.
It's a sentence for you, and it can change as your stage of life changes. Emerson's was for anyone with a talent. Micah's was for a whole people.
Yours only has to be true.

how: People who write down their real work usually keep it to one plain sentence about what they do for others, put it somewhere visible, and revisit it when their work or stage of life changes.

o: at the title on your badge.
at your talent: the talent is the call.
games.why: "each man has his own vocation. the talent is the call." the title may match it, or only sit near it.

practice: Say your job title to yourself, then set it aside and ask: when my work is going well, what am I really doing for people?
Let a few answers come and go, keeping things safe, making things clear, helping someone heal, or learn, or rest. Look for the truest one, and shape it into one plain line you could write down.

wordCard.voice: Your work. Not the title on the badge, but what you're really doing for people, written in one line. Today's word.
